summary: A declaration-sized integral-perfectoid interface on the existing Witt vectors, pretilt and Fontaine map, with a zero-ring branch and a closed characteristic-p algebraic quotient argument. The twelve accepted source aggregates and their corrections remain in a continuation register; general prismatic, mixed-characteristic and analytic endpoints remain explicit obligations. Three further lemmas isolate the elementary bounded-torsion argument for a principal Witt quotient whose generator has unit coordinate one, with no domain or nonzerodivisor premise.

nodes.title: Integral perfectoid rings
nodes.statement: Fix a prime p. A commutative ring R is integral perfectoid if it is the zero ring, or p is not a unit, R is classically p-adically complete and separated, there are π∈R and a∈R× with π^p=pa, Frobenius on R/p is surjective, and ker(θ:W(PreTilt(R,p))→R) is generated by one element. θ, PreTilt and W are the existing Mathlib constructions. The nonzero branch is exactly BMS2 Definition 4.18; completeness forces nonunit p for every nonzero R. No chosen generator, δ-structure, prism or desired comparison theorem is a field of the predicate.
hypotheses: p is prime; all rings are commutative and unital. The zero ring is allowed.
The integral predicate is independent of a topology on a Tate localization. Its p-adic completeness includes separation.
proofSteps: Use the existing PreTilt, Fontaine map and ideal span in the nonunit-p branch. The zero-ring branch is explicit because the pinned PreTilt ring instance uses a nontrivial characteristic-p quotient.
If a p-adically complete ring has p invertible, its p-adic ideal is top and IsAdicComplete.subsingleton makes it the zero ring; thus the branch condition does not exclude an object of BMS2.

The original aggregate identifier is retained for this single definition. Quasisyntomic and quasiregular semiperfectoid predicates are transferred to their DD.0/DD.5 supplier contracts; their accepted source statements remain in inheritedWork.
acceptance: The zero ring, F_p and F_p×F_p pass. Z/4, F₂[t], dual numbers and the semiperfect root quotient fail for distinct stated reasons.

nodes.statement: If p is not a unit in the classically p-complete ring R, integral perfectoidness is equivalent to the three remaining BMS2 conditions: π^p=pa for a unit a, surjective Frobenius on ModP R p, and principal ker θ.
hypotheses: p prime; the actual nonunit-p and IsAdicComplete instances are supplied.
proofSteps: The nonunit assumption rules out the subsingleton branch, because every element of a zero ring is a unit.
Unpack the existential proof instances and use proof irrelevance; the Fontaine map and its ideal do not depend on which proofs supply the instances.

nodes.title: Units in inverse perfection
nodes.statement: For a ring R of characteristic p and x∈Perfection(R,p), x is a unit if and only if its zeroth coordinate is a unit.
hypotheses: p prime; R a commutative ring of characteristic p; no surjectivity of its Frobenius is assumed.
proofSteps: A ring map preserves units, giving the forward implication.
If x₀ is a unit, each x_n is a unit because x_n^(p^n)=x₀. Their inverses form a compatible Frobenius sequence; pointwise multiplication exhibits the inverse of x in the existing Perfection ring.
acceptance: A sequence with zeroth coordinate 1 is a unit. This is inverse-limit perfection, not adjoining roots by a direct limit.

nodes.title: Units in Witt vectors over a perfect ring
nodes.statement: For a perfect ring k of characteristic p, w∈W(k) is a unit if and only if w₀ is a unit of k.
hypotheses: k is an arbitrary perfect commutative ring of characteristic p, not necessarily a field.
proofSteps: The constant-coefficient map preserves units. For the converse lift an inverse of w₀ through the surjective constant-coefficient map.

The product differs from 1 by an element of (p), by the baseline kernel formula. Witt p-adic completeness puts (p) in the Jacobson radical. The baseline Jacobson unit criterion makes the product a unit, and hence w is a unit.
acceptance: p is not a unit in W(k) when k has characteristic exactly p; 1+p is a unit.

nodes.title: The first Witt product coordinate in characteristic p
nodes.statement: For x,y∈W(k) with k of characteristic p, (xy)₁=x₀^p y₁+x₁ y₀^p.
hypotheses: p prime; k a commutative characteristic-p ring. Perfection of k is not needed.
proofSteps: Compute the first two universal Witt multiplication polynomials over the integer polynomial ring using ghost degrees zero and one. The degree-one expression is x₀^p y₁+x₁ y₀^p+p x₁y₁.
Evaluate in k; its characteristic-p hypothesis kills the last term. Cancellation of p is used only in the universal torsion-free polynomial calculation.
acceptance: The formula remains valid over nonreduced characteristic-p rings; it must not be asserted over an arbitrary mixed-characteristic coefficient ring.

nodes.title: A principal θ-kernel in characteristic p is generated by p
nodes.statement: Let R have characteristic p. Assume the pinned completeness and nonunit-p instances and that ker θ is principal. Then ker θ=(p) inside W(PreTilt(R,p)). Frobenius surjectivity on R is not required for this implication.
hypotheses: p prime; R a commutative characteristic-p ring with the indicated instances.
proofSteps: Choose ξ generating ker θ. Since p maps to zero, write p=ξa. The existing θ-mod-p formula gives c₀(ξ₀)=0, where c₀:PreTilt(R,p)→R/p.
Apply c₀ to the first Witt product coordinate. Since p₁=1, obtain 1=c₀(ξ₁)c₀(a₀)^p. Thus c₀(a₀) is a unit.

The inverse-perfection unit criterion makes a₀ a unit; the perfect-Witt unit criterion makes a a unit. Therefore ξ and p generate the same ideal. This is the characteristic-p specialization of the generator argument, so no general prism correspondence is imported.
acceptance: No p-torsion cancellation is performed in R. The conclusion concerns the kernel in its Witt ring.

nodes.title: Injectivity of the characteristic-p tilt projection
nodes.statement: Under the hypotheses of the preceding kernel lemma, the zeroth-coordinate map PreTilt(R,p)→R/p is injective.
hypotheses: R has characteristic exactly p; ker θ principal; existing θ hypotheses.
proofSteps: If x has zeroth coordinate zero, θ([x]) is zero because R/p=R and the baseline θ-mod-p formula identifies its reduction.
Then [x] belongs to ker θ=(p). The baseline constant-coefficient kernel formula forces x=0. A ring homomorphism with zero kernel is injective.

nodes.title: Naturality of the multiplicative untilt
nodes.statement: For a ring map f:R→S between classically p-complete rings with p nonunit, let g:R/p→S/p commute with the quotient maps and f. For every x∈PreTilt(R,p), f(x♯)=(Perfection.map(g)(x))♯.
hypotheses: p prime; the commuting reduction square is a hypothesis and is retained in the suggested signature.
proofSteps: Choose lifts of each coordinate of x. Their images under f lift the corresponding coordinates of Perfection.map(g)(x), by the commuting square.
The baseline Teichmüller congruence determines each sharp modulo p^(n+1) by the p^n-th power of a lift. Apply f to those congruences.
p-adic separation of S identifies the two elements. No topological structure is added: a ring map sends p^nR into p^nS.

nodes.title: Naturality of Fontaine’s map
nodes.statement: With f and g as in untilt naturality, f(θ_R(w))=θ_S(W(g♭)(w)) for all w∈W(PreTilt(R,p)).
hypotheses: The two rings are classically p-complete, p is nonunit in each, and g is the map induced by f modulo p.
proofSteps: Reduce both ring maps to S/p^n. The prime is nilpotent in that target.
Use the baseline equality criterion for maps out of Witt vectors into a p-nilpotent ring: equality on Teichmüller representatives suffices. θ([x])=x♯ and untilt naturality give that equality.
Apply p-adic separation of S. The nilpotence hypothesis is used only after reduction, never asserted in S.

nodes.title: Invariance under ring equivalence
nodes.statement: For every ring equivalence e:R≃S, integral perfectoidness of R at p is equivalent to that of S at p.
hypotheses: p prime; commutative unital rings; the zero ring is included.
proofSteps: Transport the subsingleton case directly. Otherwise transport completeness along the bijection of p-adic congruence systems, and the root/unit and Frobenius-surjectivity conditions along e.

The induced maps modulo p, on inverse perfection, and on Witt vectors are equivalences because the inverse ring map gives their inverses. θ naturality identifies the two kernels, so principal generation transfers in both directions.
acceptance: Changing the presentation of F_p or its finite product does not change perfectoidness.

nodes.title: Integral perfectoidness in characteristic p
nodes.statement: A commutative ring of characteristic exactly p is integral perfectoid if and only if it satisfies Mathlib PerfectRing R p, namely bijectivity of the p-th-power map.
hypotheses: p prime; characteristic exactly p gives a nonzero ring. The zero-ring statement is separately part of the definition API.
proofSteps: For a perfectoid R, use the nontrivial criterion. Frobenius surjectivity gives surjectivity of the tilt projection by Perfection.coeff_surjective. The principal-kernel lemma gives injectivity. Thus R/p=R is isomorphic to its perfect inverse perfection.
Conversely, if R is perfect, the projection from its inverse perfection is bijective: existence uses successive unique roots, and uniqueness follows from injectivity of their powers.

Under R/p=R, the existing θ formula is the constant-coefficient map followed by this bijection. Its kernel is (p) by the baseline Witt kernel formula. The p-adic ideal is zero, so R is complete, and π=0 with unit 1 supplies the root condition.
acceptance: F_p×F_p passes; F₂[t] and F₂[ε]/ε² fail. The semiperfect quotient of the perfect closure of F₂[t] also fails.

sources.locator: Example 3.15, p.24, with Lemma 3.10 proof, p.23

nodes.title: Surjectivity of powers on a quotient
nodes.statement: If the p-th-power function on a commutative ring R is surjective, its p-th-power function on R/I is surjective for every ideal I.
hypotheses: p prime in the roadmap specialization. The argument itself needs no characteristic or reducedness assumption.
proofSteps: Lift a quotient element to r∈R using the existing surjective quotient map. Choose a p-th root s of r. Its class is a p-th root of the given quotient element.
acceptance: It holds even for the semiperfect nonreduced quotient A/(t), so surjectivity alone cannot be the target perfectoid criterion.

nodes.title: Perfect quotients of a perfect characteristic-p ring
nodes.statement: For a perfect ring R of characteristic p and any ideal I, PerfectRing(R/I,p) holds if and only if I is radical. This includes I=R and its zero quotient.
hypotheses: p prime; R a perfect commutative ring of characteristic exactly p; no properness or finite-generation condition on I.
proofSteps: The quotient power map is surjective by quotient-frobenius-surjective. If I is radical then R/I is reduced; split off the zero ring, and in the nonzero case give the quotient characteristic p and apply PerfectRing.ofSurjective.

Conversely, bijectivity of the p-th power implies that no nonzero element of the quotient is nilpotent: choose p^n at least the nilpotence exponent and use injectivity repeatedly. The existing radical/reduced-quotient equivalence gives radicality of I.
acceptance: The top ideal gives the zero ring, which still has bijective p-th power. Nonradical ideals fail injectivity.

nodes.title: The radical quotient is integral perfectoid
nodes.statement: For a perfect characteristic-p ring R and any ideal I, R/√I is integral perfectoid at p, including the zero quotient.
hypotheses: p prime; R perfect of characteristic p.
proofSteps: The radical is radical in the existing ideal API. The perfect-quotient criterion gives PerfectRing(R/√I,p).
If the quotient is zero use the explicit zero-ring branch. Otherwise the map from R gives characteristic p, and the characteristic-p perfectoid criterion applies.
acceptance: For I=0 the quotient is R; for I=R it is the zero ring.

nodes.title: Perfectoidization of a characteristic-p quotient
nodes.statement: Let R be a perfect ring of characteristic p and I an arbitrary ideal. For every integral perfectoid ring T and ring map f:R→T killing I, there is a unique ring map g:R/√I→T with g composed with the quotient map equal to f. Together with the preceding perfectoidness lemma and the existing surjective map R/I→R/√I, this identifies R/√I as the universal integral perfectoid ring under R/I.
hypotheses: No characteristic assumption is imposed on T: the given ring map forces p=0 in T. The zero target is allowed.
proofSteps: If T is zero the factorization is unique. Otherwise f(p)=0 gives characteristic p; the integral-perfectoid criterion makes T perfect, hence reduced.
Every element of √I maps to a nilpotent and hence to zero in T. Apply the existing Ideal.Quotient.lift to f.

The quotient map from R is surjective, so the lift is unique. Apply Ideal.quotientMap_surjective to the identity of R and I≤√I for the surjectivity from R/I. No transfinite prism, completed base change or André theorem enters this specialization.
acceptance: Surjectivity is a statement about the canonical quotient map, not an abstract existence of a perfectoid target. It works for infinitely generated I.

sources.match: Explicit characteristic-p proof of the universal-property and surjectivity specialization; no claim to close the mixed-characteristic theorem.

nodes.title: The ideal of all roots of a principal element
nodes.statement: In a perfect ring R of characteristic p, for f∈R the ideal generated by φ^(−n)(f), n≥0, equals √(f). Roots here are supplied by the inverse of the existing Frobenius ring equivalence.
hypotheses: p prime; R perfect of characteristic p. This is an algebraic ideal with no topology attached.
proofSteps: Every listed root has p^n-th power f, so belongs to √(f).
If x^m belongs to (f), choose n with p^n≥m, and write x^(p^n)=fc. Apply the inverse n-th Frobenius to obtain x=φ^(−n)(f)φ^(−n)(c), proving membership in the root ideal.
Both inclusions hold for arbitrary f, including zero and units. The fixed-root sequence has exact compatibility, not independently chosen roots.
acceptance: For f=0 the ideal is zero; for f=1 it is top; every compatible root maps to zero in the radical quotient.

nodes.title: Which algebraic quotients stay integral perfectoid
nodes.statement: For a perfect characteristic-p ring R and any ideal I, R/I is integral perfectoid at p if and only if I is radical.
hypotheses: p prime; characteristic-p perfect source; arbitrary ideal, including top.
proofSteps: Split the zero quotient. The ideal is then top and radical, and the zero ring is integral perfectoid.
For a nonzero quotient, transfer characteristic p along the quotient map. Apply the characteristic-p integral-perfectoid criterion followed by the perfect-quotient radical criterion.
acceptance: For A=F₂[t^(1/2^∞)], the ideal (t) is not radical because t^(1/2) is outside it but has square in it. Its quotient is semiperfect but not integral perfectoid.

nodes.title: Detecting a factor modulo p from a Witt product
nodes.statement: If p squared divides xi times g in W(k), and Witt coordinate one of xi is a unit, then p divides g. There is no condition on coordinate zero of xi and no assumed nonzerodivisor property of xi.
hypotheses: p is prime; k is a commutative perfect ring of characteristic p; xi belongs to W(k); its Witt coordinate xi_1 is a unit in k.
proofSteps: Apply the pinned Teichmuller expansion theorem at precision p squared to xi and g. Write xi=[a0]+p[a1] modulo p squared and g=[b0]+p[b1] modulo p squared, where a1 is inverse Frobenius applied to xi_1, hence is a unit. These are Teichmuller p-adic digits, not raw Witt coordinates.

Multiply these two congruences. Multiplicativity of Teichmuller representatives gives xi*g=[a0*b0]+p*([a0*b1]+[a1*b0]) modulo p squared. Reducing with constantCoeff yields a0*b0=0, so the first displayed Teichmuller term vanishes.

Cancel one p using the pinned p-torsionfreeness of W(k), then reduce again with constantCoeff to obtain a0*b1+a1*b0=0. Multiplying by b0 and using the first relation gives a1*(b0^2)=0. Since a1 is a unit, b0 squared=0.
As p is at least two, b0 to the pth power vanishes. Injectivity of Frobenius on the perfect ring k gives b0=0. The pinned first-coordinate ideal-membership criterion then gives p divides g.
acceptance: For xi=p, the condition reduces to p squared dividing p*g if and only if p divides g; xi_1=1.

nodes.title: One-step p-saturation of a principal Witt ideal
nodes.statement: If p squared times f belongs to the ordinary ideal generated by xi in W(k), then p times f belongs to that ideal, under the unit-coordinate hypothesis on xi.
hypotheses: p is prime; k is a commutative perfect ring of characteristic p; xi belongs to W(k); its Witt coordinate xi_1 is a unit in k.
proofSteps: Write p squared times f=xi*g using the existing principal-ideal membership theorem.

The product-detection lemma gives g=p*h. Rearrange the equality as p*(p*f)=p*(xi*h), and use p-torsionfreeness of the Witt ring to cancel p. The result p*f=xi*h proves membership in the same ideal. No cancellation of xi is used.
acceptance: The quotient W(k)/(p) is killed by p for any perfect k of characteristic p, including a product of fields; no domain hypothesis is needed.

nodes.title: Bounded torsion in a principal Witt quotient
nodes.statement: For Q=W(k)/(xi), every x in Q and every nonnegative integer n satisfy: if p to the nth power times x is zero, then p times x is zero. Thus the p-primary torsion of Q is already killed by p. This is a sufficient criterion, not a characterization of all principal ideals with this property.
hypotheses: p is prime; k is a commutative perfect ring of characteristic p; xi belongs to W(k); its Witt coordinate xi_1 is a unit in k.
proofSteps: Choose a representative f of x using the existing quotient projection. The relation p squared times x=0 is equivalent to p squared times f lying in (xi), so one-step saturation gives p times x=0.

For arbitrary n, n=0 forces x=0 and n=1 is the hypothesis itself. For n at least two, apply the square-step result to p to the (n-2) power times x; this lowers the annihilating exponent by one. Induction finishes.

To use the result for a perfectoid ring, separately establish its representation W(R-flat)/(xi) and the unit coefficient of a chosen kernel generator. These source hypotheses are not inferred from principal generation alone.
acceptance: In W(F_2)/(4), the class of one is killed by 4 but not by 2. The generator 4 has Witt coordinate one equal to zero, so it is excluded by the theorem.

nodes.title: Integral perfectoid, semiperfectoid, quasisyntomic and quasiregular semiperfectoid rings
nodes.statement: (BMS2 4.18) A ring R is perfectoid if it is p-adically complete, there is π ∈ R with π^p = pu for a unit u, Frobenius is surjective on R/p, and ker(θ: A_inf(R) = W(R♭) → R) is principal; then ker θ is generated by a nonzerodivisor ξ = p + [π♭]^p α, L_{R/Z_p} has p-complete Tor-amplitude in degree −1 with p-completion R[1], and R[p^∞] = R[p]. (BMS2 4.10) A is quasisyntomic if p-complete with bounded p^∞-torsion and L_{A/Z_p} has p-complete Tor-amplitude in [−1, 0]; a map of such rings is a quasisyntomic cover if p-completely faithfully flat with p-complete Tor-amplitude of L_{B/A} in [−1, 0]. (BS22 7.1) S is semiperfectoid if it is a derived p-complete ring admitting a surjection from a perfectoid ring; it is quasiregular if in addition it has bounded p^∞-torsion and L_{S/Z_p}[−1] is p-completely flat over S, in which case S is classically p-complete. (BMS2 4.20, 4.22; the identification with BS22 Notation 7.1 is a packet-authored reconciliation via Remarks 4.21-4.22) S is quasiregular semiperfectoid iff quasisyntomic, receiving a map from a perfectoid ring, with S/p semiperfect; conditions (2)-(3) may be replaced by the existence of a surjection from a perfectoid ring.
hypotheses: All completions are p-adic (BMS2) or derived p-adic (BS22 Notation 7.1); BS22 asks only derived p-completeness for semiperfectoid, and Notation 7.1 records that quasiregularity forces classical p-completeness.
Perfectoid here is the integral notion of BMS1 §3, not the Tate-ring notion of PerfectoidSpaces:P1; the comparison for R^+ inside a perfectoid Tate ring is not proved in the sources read (gap).
proofSteps: BMS2 Remark 4.21: semiperfectness of S/p gives Ω¹_{(S/p)/F_p} = 0, so L_{S/R} ⊗^L S/p ∈ D^{≤ −1} for any R → S. For S ∈ QSyn, whose L_{S/Z_p} has p-complete Tor-amplitude in [−1, 0], this places the Tor-amplitude in degree −1.

BMS2 Remark 4.22: given R → S with R perfectoid and S/p semiperfect, R ⊗̂_{Z_p} W(S♭) is perfectoid and surjects onto S (S♭ the inverse-limit perfection of S/p), so the two formulations of the definition agree.
acceptance: The ϖ-adic completion of R^+/(I ∩ R^+) for R^+ integral perfectoid is semiperfectoid (Remark 7.5), and R⟨X^{1/p^∞}⟩/(X − f) for perfectoid R is quasiregular semiperfectoid (proof of Prop. 7.10).

A perfectoid ring is quasiregular semiperfectoid with L_{R/Z_p}^∧ = R[1] (Example 4.24, Proposition 4.19). O_C/p is quasiregular semiperfectoid, and a test must not classify it otherwise. It is p-complete with bounded p-torsion, a quotient of the perfectoid O_C by the nonzerodivisor p, and L_{(O_C/p)/O_C} ≅ (p)/(p²)[1] is p-completely flat in degree −1, so BMS2 Lemma 4.25 applies (the regular-quotient formula is DD.0 content).

nodes.title: Maps out of a perfect prism are determined by their reduction: (A_inf(R), ker θ) is initial in (R)_Δ
nodes.statement: Let (A, I) be a perfect prism with perfectoid ring R = A/I. For any prism (B, J), any ring map A/I → B/J lifts uniquely to a map of prisms (A, I) → (B, J). Hence (R)_Δ = (R/A)_Δ. The dual statement fails: a prism (A, I) may admit several maps to a perfect prism (B, J) with the same reduction.
hypotheses: (A, I) perfect (φ_A bijective); B and B/J derived p-complete; B may have p-torsion, which is why being a δ-map must be checked separately.

Uses that L_{A/Z_p} vanishes after derived p-completion because A is the ring of Witt vectors of a perfect F_p-algebra. The source states this without proof; identifying a perfect prism with W(A/p) is Corollary 2.31, a packet-supplied reference.

Placement: Lemma 4.8 is an application of PR.0's perfect-prism/perfectoid-ring correspondence and rigidity, so it is filed under Q0:animated-application (which imports PR.0), not under Q0:integral-algebra (which PR.0 itself requires).
proofSteps: Deformation theory: Hom(A, B) ≅ Hom(A, B/J) ≅ Hom(A, B/(J, p)) since L_{A/Z_p}^∧ = 0 and B, B/J are derived p-complete; so A → A/I → B/J lifts uniquely to α: A → B, compatible with Frobenius lifts, with α(I) ⊂ J.

α is a δ-map: it factors uniquely through B^perf = lim_φ B → B by bijectivity of φ on A; B^perf is a perfect δ-ring, hence p-torsionfree, so the φ-equivariant map A → B^perf is automatically a δ-map, and B^perf → B is a δ-map by construction.

The proof ends there: α is a δ-map with α(I) ⊂ J, hence a map of prisms. Rigidity (Lemma 3.5, IB = J) is not used in Lemma 4.8. It is used in the proof of Proposition 7.2 ("K = dC by Lemma 3.5"), and the PR.0 rigidity link was re-targeted there by REVIEW-EXT-03.
acceptance: For R = O_C and any prism (B, J) with a map O_C → B/J, there is a unique prism map (A_inf(O_C), (ξ)) → (B, J), so the absolute prismatic site of Spf O_C is the relative site over A_inf.
The uniqueness fails for maps into perfect prisms from non-perfect prisms (remark after Lemma 4.8).

nodes.title: The category of prisms under a semiperfectoid ring has an initial object with principal ideal
nodes.statement: For a semiperfectoid ring S, the category of all prisms (A, I) with a map S → A/I has an initial object (Δ^init_S, I) with I = (d) principal. Δ^init_S is a derived (p, d)-complete δ-A_inf(R)-algebra in which d is a nonzerodivisor, obtained from B = A_inf(R){x_f | f ∈ J}/(d x_f − f | f ∈ J)_δ (J = ker(A_inf(R) → R → S)) by killing the smallest δ-stable ideal containing the d^∞-torsion, taking H^0 of the derived (p, d)-completion, and iterating transfinitely. The source identifies this category with the absolute prismatic site (Spf S)_Δ of Remark 4.7. The objects of that site are bounded prisms, whereas Δ^init_S "is not bounded in general", so Δ^init_S need not be an object of (Spf S)_Δ.
hypotheses: S = R/J' for a perfectoid ring R (surjection chosen); (A_inf(R), ker θ = (d)) is the initial prism under R (Lemma 4.8) and ker θ is principal.
Δ^init_S is not bounded in general; its perfection is the well-behaved object (Corollary 7.3).
The transfinite induction uses that derived completion commutes with ω₁-filtered colimits.

Asserted, not argued: that the transfinite torsion-removal process ends in a d-torsion-free derived (p, d)-complete ring still receiving a unique map to every (C, K), and that Remark 4.7's bounded site is the category meant.
proofSteps: Given a prism (C, K) with S → C/K, Lemma 4.8 gives a unique (A_inf(R), (d)) → (C, K) and K = dC by rigidity (Lemma 3.5); d is a nonzerodivisor in C, so each f ∈ J has a unique quotient f/d ∈ C.

Freely adjoining x_f with d x_f = f in δ-rings gives a unique δ-map B → C; since C is d-torsionfree it factors through B/B[d^∞]_δ, and since C is derived (p, d)-complete and classical, through H^0 of the derived (p, d)-completion.

The completed quotient may acquire new d-torsion; transfinite iteration (completion commuting with ω₁-filtered colimits) produces Δ^init_S with d a nonzerodivisor and still a unique map to (C, K); d is distinguished, so (Δ^init_S, (d)) is a prism.
R = A_inf(R)/d → Δ^init_S/d factors through S because all elements of J become divisible by d.
acceptance: For S = R perfectoid, Δ^init_S = A_inf(R) by Lemma 4.8, since (A_inf(R), ker θ) is already initial among prisms under R.
For S = R/(f) with f admitting compatible p-power roots, Corollary 7.3 and the proof of Theorem 7.4 together give that the p-adic completion of (Δ^init_S)_perf/I is the p-completion of R/(f^{1/p^∞}).

nodes.title: Universal perfectoid ring S_perfd under a semiperfectoid ring
nodes.statement: For semiperfectoid S there is a universal perfectoid ring S_perfd with a map S → S_perfd (every map from S to a perfectoid ring factors uniquely through it), namely S_perfd = p-adic completion of (Δ^init_S)_perf / I, where (Δ^init_S)_perf is the completed perfection of the initial prism.
hypotheses: Uses the equivalence between perfectoid rings and perfect prisms (Theorem 3.10; supplied by PrismaticCohomology:PR.0/perfect-prisms-perfectoid-rings) so that perfectoid rings under S are perfect prisms under (Δ^init_S, I).

Uses Lemma 3.9: the completed perfection (A_∞, IA_∞) of a prism is the universal perfect prism under it, IA_perf = (d) with d, p nonzerodivisors and A_perf/d[p^∞] = A_perf/d[p]; the derived and classical (p, I)-completions agree.
proofSteps: Perfectoid rings S_perfd with S → S_perfd correspond to perfect prisms (A, I) with R → A/I factoring through S, i.e. to perfect prisms under (Δ^init_S, I).
Lemma 3.9 identifies the universal perfect prism under (Δ^init_S, I) as its completed perfection; reduce modulo I and note the quotient is p-adically complete (bounded p-torsion).
acceptance: For S perfectoid, S_perfd = S.
Theorem 7.4 asserts S → S_perfd is surjective; before that theorem only the universal property is known.

nodes.title: Derived prismatic cohomology by left Kan extension, with its Hodge-Tate filtration and formal properties
nodes.statement: For a bounded prism (A, I), the functor R ↦ Δ_{R/A} on p-completely smooth A/I-algebras (valued in commutative algebras in (p, I)-complete objects of D(A) with φ_A-semilinear Frobenius) is left Kan extended to all derived p-complete simplicial commutative A/I-algebras. The Hodge-Tate comparison (Theorem 6.3) yields on Δ̄_{R/A} := Δ_{R/A} ⊗^L_A A/I an exhaustive increasing N-indexed filtration with gr^i = derived p-completion of ∧^i L_{R/(A/I)}{−i}[−i]. Consequences: (1) agreement with Δ_{R/A} for p-completely smooth R; (2) R ↦ Δ_{R/A} is a sheaf for the p-completely etale topology; (3) for perfect (A, I) it is a quasisyntomic sheaf on quasisyntomic A/I-algebras; (4) base change Δ_{R_B/B} ≅ Δ_{R/A} ⊗̂^L_A B for maps of bounded prisms (A, I) → (B, J), R_B the derived p-completion of R ⊗^L_A B; (5) the functor is symmetric monoidal and commutes with all colimits.
hypotheses: (A, I) bounded; left Kan extension in the sense of Lurie HTT §5.5.9 along the inclusion of p-completely smooth algebras into derived p-complete simplicial commutative A/I-algebras.

This construction is owned by PrismaticCohomology:PR.2 according to stage Q2 ('Import PR.2's independent extension'); no PR.2 node exists yet in the PrismaticCohomology draft, so the construction is recorded here as read (see gap).
Properties (2)-(5) are asserted as 'immediate consequences' of the Hodge-Tate filtration; the source gives no further argument.
proofSteps: Define Δ_{R/A} as the left Kan extension; on smooth algebras nothing changes (1).

The Hodge-Tate comparison for smooth algebras (Theorem 6.3: Ω^i_{R/(A/I)} ≅ H^i(Δ̄_{R/A}){i}) left-Kan-extends to the filtration with graded pieces the completed derived exterior powers of the cotangent complex, since ∧^i L extends Ω^i.

(2)-(5) are stated as "immediate consequences". Packet-authored reading: they follow from the filtration by etale/quasisyntomic descent of completed derived exterior powers of the cotangent complex, base change of L, and colimit preservation of the associated graded. For (3) the source points only to a variant for derived de Rham cohomology in characteristic p ([BMS19, Example 5.11], unread).
acceptance: For R = A/I⟨X⟩, gr^1 = R{−1}[−1] and the filtration recovers the Hodge-Tate comparison Ω¹ ≅ H¹(Δ̄){1}.
For R with L_{R/(A/I)}[−1] p-completely flat (e.g. quasiregular semiperfectoid over a perfect prism) all gr^i are discrete, so Δ̄_{R/A} is discrete (used in 7.10).

nodes.title: When Δ_{R/A} is discrete it is a δ-ring, a prism over (A, I), and weakly initial with an idempotent retract that is initial
nodes.statement: Let (A, I) be a bounded prism and R a derived p-complete simplicial A/I-algebra with Δ_{R/A} concentrated in degree 0. Then (1) the φ_A-linear Frobenius on Δ_{R/A} lifts naturally to a δ-A-structure; (2) (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) is a prism over (A, I) with a map R → Δ̄_{R/A}; (3) the category of prisms (B, J) over (A, I) with R → B/J has an initial object, (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) is weakly initial, and the initial object is the retract of an idempotent endomorphism of (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}). (Lemma 7.8) In an idempotent complete category C, if the identity factors through C_{X\} → C via F: C → C_{X\}, then F(X) is an idempotent of X whose retract is initial in C.
hypotheses: Discreteness of Δ_{R/A} (hence of Δ̄_{R/A} = Δ_{R/A} ⊗^L_A A/I for (2)).

The δ-structure is obtained from the functorial Čech-Alexander model F_A(R) and the map F_A(R) → W_2(F_A(R)) classifying δ-structures, together with the pullback square W_2(B) = B ×_{B ⊗^L F_p} B for simplicial commutative rings.
BS22 conjectures that (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) is itself initial; only weak initiality plus the retract is proved.

Lemma 7.8 is stated for an idempotent complete category. The source applies it to (R/A)_Δ without checking idempotent completeness; this is a gap. In part (3), "Using the argument from part (1), one shows that this is in fact a map of δ-rings" is asserted.
proofSteps: (1) Build the map Δ_{R/A} ≅ colim lim F_A(R) → colim lim W_2(F_A(R)) of E_∞-rings over A → W_2(A), splitting restriction; identify the target with W_2(Δ_{R/A}) using the pullback square and discreteness; this is a δ-structure refining φ_R.
(2) Immediate from derived (p, I)-completeness and discreteness of Δ̄_{R/A}.

(3) For any (B, J) in (R/A)_Δ, resolving R by p-completely ind-smooth R_i and writing Δ_{R/A} = colim_{Δ^op} lim_{C ∈ (R_•/A)_Δ} C, restrict the limit to the compatible objects defined by (B, J) to get a functorial δ-map Δ_{R/A} → B; conclude by Lemma 7.8 (faithful F, epimorphism X → X', at most one and at least one map X' → Y).
acceptance: Lemma 7.8 applied to C = (R/A)_Δ with X = (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) gives the initial object as a retract.
In Example 7.9 and Proposition 7.10 the idempotent is shown to be the identity.

nodes.title: For a Koszul-regular quotient R = A/(I, f_1, ..., f_r) with bounded p-torsion, Δ_{R/A} is the prismatic envelope and initial
nodes.statement: Fix a bounded prism (A, I) and R = A/J with J = (I, f_1, ..., f_r), f_1, ..., f_r Koszul-regular on A/I, R with bounded p-torsion. Then Δ_{R/A} is concentrated in degree 0 and I-torsionfree, and (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) is the initial object of (R/A)_Δ; locally where I = (d), Δ_{R/A} = A{f_1/d, ..., f_r/d}^∧ (the prismatic envelope A{J/I}^∧ of Proposition 3.13).
hypotheses: Koszul-regularity of f_1, ..., f_r on A/I and bounded p-torsion of R; principal I after localization on Spf A.

Imports: Proposition 3.13 (prismatic envelopes of regular ideals; supplied by PrismaticCohomology:PR.0/regular-prismatic-envelopes), Lemma 7.7, the Hodge-Tate filtration, and a standard free-resolution computation cited to [Bha12, Claim 3.30] (unread).

Also used: Lemma 7.7(1)-(2) to regard (Δ_{R/A}, IΔ_{R/A}) as an object of (R/A)_Δ, and the assertion "the formation of both sides commutes with arbitrary base change" (Construction 7.6(4) for Δ, free δ-adjunction for B).
proofSteps: Δ_{R/A} is discrete and I-torsionfree by the Hodge-Tate filtration (gr^i are completed exterior powers of L_{R/(A/I)} = J/(J² + I)[1]), so it is an object of (R/A)_Δ.

Base change reduces the comparison B := A{f_i/d}^∧ → Δ_{R/A} to the universal case A = Z_p{d, f_1, ..., f_r}[δ(d)^{-1}]^∧, where A/I and R are p-torsionfree and f_1, ..., f_r is p-completely regular relative to A_0/I_0 for (A_0, I_0) = (Z_p{d}[δ(d)^{-1}]^∧, (d)); Proposition 3.13 identifies B with the prismatic envelope, discrete and initial in (R/A)_Δ.

B → Δ_{R/A} has a retraction by Lemma 7.7, so B/IB → Δ̄_{R/A} has p-torsionfree cokernel; it suffices that B/IB[1/p] → Δ̄_{R/A}[1/p] is surjective, which holds because Δ̄_{R/A}[1/p] is generated as a Banach R[1/p]-algebra by gr^1 = J/(J² + I){−1} and J/I maps onto it.
acceptance: R = A/(I, f) with f a nonzerodivisor on A/I and R of bounded p-torsion: Δ_{R/A} = A{f/d}^∧, and the initial prism is obtained by adjoining f/d.
The example is the engine of Proposition 7.10 via the rings T = R⟨X_1^{1/p^∞}, ..., X_r^{1/p^∞}⟩/(X_1 − f_1, ..., X_r − f_r).

nodes.title: For quasiregular semiperfectoid S, Δ_{S/A} is discrete, equals the initial prism Δ^init_S independently of the perfectoid R, and S → Δ̄_S is p-completely faithfully flat
nodes.statement: Let S be quasiregular semiperfectoid, R → S any map from a perfectoid ring, (A, I) = (A_inf(R), ker θ). Then Δ_{S/A} is discrete, (Δ_{S/A}, IΔ_{S/A}) is the initial prism Δ^init_S with a map S → Δ^init_S/I (so Δ_{S/A} does not depend on R), and S → Δ̄_{S/A} = Δ_{S/A}/I is p-completely faithfully flat. Notation: Δ_S := Δ^init_S = Δ_{S/A}.
hypotheses: S quasiregular in the sense of Notation 7.1 (bounded p^∞-torsion and L_{S/Z_p}[−1] p-completely flat) and semiperfectoid; R perfectoid mapping to S, not necessarily surjectively. The proof uses the consequence that L_{S/R}[−1] is p-completely flat.

Uses the Hodge-Tate filtration (all gr^i = completed ∧^i L_{S/R}[−i]{−i} p-completely flat, hence discrete), Lemma 7.7(3), Example 7.9, and the invariance of Δ_{S/A} under R ↦ R⟨Y_i^{1/p^∞}⟩ and under A ↦ A_inf(R⟨X^{1/p^∞}⟩).

Implicit in the reduction: the idempotents of Lemma 7.7(3) are natural in S. This is needed so that surjectivity of Δ_{S'} → Δ_S and the filtered colimit S' = colim T transfer "idempotent = id". The source also writes Δ_{S/R} for Δ_{S/A}.
proofSteps: Discreteness and faithful flatness: the completed derived exterior powers ∧^i L_{S/R}[−i] are p-completely flat S-modules, so the Hodge-Tate filtration exhibits Δ̄_{S/A} as discrete and p-completely faithfully flat over S (source). That Δ_{S/A} is then discrete follows by derived (p, I)-completeness (packet-authored step).

Initiality: it suffices that the idempotent of Lemma 7.7(3) is the identity. Replace R by R⟨Y_i^{1/p^∞} | i ∈ I⟩ (no change to cotangent complexes) to make R → S surjective with kernel generated by {f_j}; S' = R⟨X_j^{1/p^∞}⟩/(X_j − f_j)^∧ → S is surjective on rings and on cotangent complexes, so Δ_{S'/R} → Δ_{S/R} is surjective and it suffices to treat S'.

S' is a filtered colimit of T = R⟨X_1^{1/p^∞}, ..., X_r^{1/p^∞}⟩/(X_1 − f_1, ..., X_r − f_r), and Δ_{T/A} ≅ Δ_{T/A'} for A' = A_inf(R⟨X^{1/p^∞}⟩) compatibly with idempotents; Example 7.9 (T is a Koszul-regular quotient of A'/I) shows the idempotent is the identity.
acceptance: O_C/p is quasiregular semiperfectoid (see the Q0:integral-algebra node), so Proposition 7.10 applies to it. For S = R/(f) with R perfectoid, f admitting compatible p-power roots, f a nonzerodivisor on R and R/f of bounded p-torsion, Δ_S is the completed prismatic envelope A_inf(R){[f♭]/d}^∧ (Example 7.9 with r = 1 and lift [f♭] of f).
Independence of R: Δ_{S/A_inf(R)} ≅ Δ_{S/A_inf(R')} for any two perfectoid rings mapping to S.

nodes.title: A quasisyntomic A/I-algebra admits a prism (B, IB) over (A, I) with R → B/IB p-completely faithfully flat; flatness of the (perfected) prism
nodes.statement: Let (A, I) be a bounded prism and R a quasisyntomic A/I-algebra. Then there is (B → B/IB ← R) ∈ (R/A)_Δ with R → B/IB p-completely faithfully flat. Consequently (1) (A, I) → (B, IB) is a flat map of prisms, faithfully flat if A/I → R is p-completely faithfully flat; (2) if A is perfect, (A, I) → (B, IB)_perf is flat, faithfully flat under the same condition.
hypotheses: R quasisyntomic over A/I; the cover S := A/I⟨x_j^{1/p^∞}⟩ ⊗̂^L_{A/I⟨x_j⟩} R built from a surjection A/I⟨x_j | j ∈ J⟩ → R is a quasisyntomic cover with S/p relatively semiperfect over A/(I, p), so L^∧_{S/(A/I)}[−1] is p-completely flat. The source asserts both properties with "It is easy to see" and "In particular".

The prism B = Δ_{S/A} is produced by the first half of the proof of Proposition 7.10 and Lemma 7.7 (discreteness gives the δ-structure); (2) uses passage to filtered colimits (perfection = colim over φ).
proofSteps: Construct S by formally extracting p-power roots of a set of generators x_j; R → S is a quasisyntomic cover and A/(I, p) → S/p is relatively semiperfect (quotient of a flat algebra with bijective relative Frobenius), so Ω¹_{S/(A/I)}/p = 0 and L^∧_{S/(A/I)}[−1] is p-completely flat.
As in Proposition 7.10, the Hodge-Tate filtration shows Δ_{S/A} is discrete and S → Δ̄_{S/A} p-completely faithfully flat; Lemma 7.7 makes B = Δ_{S/A} a prism over (A, I).

(1): A/I → R → S → B/IB is a composite of p-completely flat maps (faithfully flat if the first is); (2): perfection is a filtered colimit of Frobenius twists, preserving (faithful) flatness. The passage from p-complete flatness of A/I → B/IB to (p, I)-complete flatness of A → B is not written out.
acceptance: For R = A/I itself the construction gives a faithfully flat prism cover in which every element of a generating set has compatible p-power roots.

Examples of Example 7.12's covers R → R_∞ (footnote 12, which belongs to Example 7.12, not to Proposition 7.11): for a perfect crystalline prism take R_∞ the perfection of R; with etale coordinates take R_∞ = R[y_i^{1/p^∞}]^∧/(y_i − x_i).

nodes.title: Andre's flatness lemma: every perfectoid ring has a p-completely faithfully flat absolutely integrally closed perfectoid extension
nodes.statement: Let R be a perfectoid ring. There is a p-completely faithfully flat map R → S of perfectoid rings with S absolutely integrally closed (every monic polynomial over S has a root); in particular every element of S admits a compatible system of p-power roots. The map can moreover be chosen to be an ind-syntomic cover modulo p (Remark 7.15, sketched).
hypotheses: R perfectoid, written as A/I for a perfect prism (A, I) (Theorem 3.10).
R̃ := p-complete R-algebra obtained by formally adjoining roots of all monic polynomials over R is a quasisyntomic cover of R (asserted, not proved in the source).

Transfinite iteration of R ↦ R_1 and the perfectoidness/faithful flatness at limit stages are asserted in one sentence; the stage text asks for completeness, perfectoidness, faithful flatness and size bounds at limit stages explicitly.
proofSteps: Proposition 7.11(2) applied to R̃ gives a perfect prism (B, IB) over (A, I) with R̃ → B/IB =: R_1 such that R → R̃ → R_1 is p-completely faithfully flat; R_1 is perfectoid and every monic polynomial over R has a root in R_1. (Proposition 7.11(2) gives flatness of (A, I) → (B, IB)_perf; the proof of Theorem 7.14 writes "perfect prism (B, IB)" for this perfection.)
Transfinitely iterate R ↦ R_1 to obtain a quasisyntomic cover R → R' with R' perfectoid and absolutely integrally closed.

nodes.title: Closed perfectoid quotients: the vanishing locus of an ideal in an affinoid perfectoid space is strongly Zariski closed
nodes.statement: Let X = Spa(R, R^+) be affinoid perfectoid (R a perfectoid Tate ring with pseudo-uniformizer ϖ, R^+ ⊂ R° open and integrally closed) and I ⊂ R an ideal. Let S be the ϖ-adic completion of R^+/(I ∩ R^+); S is semiperfectoid, R' := S_perfd[1/ϖ] is a perfectoid Tate ring which is a quotient of R, every map from R to a perfectoid ring vanishing on I factors uniquely through R', and the vanishing locus of I in X is the strongly Zariski closed subset Spa(R', R'^+) with R'^+ the minimal open integrally closed subring of R' containing the image of R^+. Hence (ECD 5.8) every Zariski closed immersion Z → X (closed immersion whose image is the zero locus of an ideal) is strongly Zariski closed (Z = Spa(S, S^+) affinoid with R → S surjective and S^+ the integral closure of R^+ in S); the claim in [Sch15, Remark II.2.4] that the notions differ was erroneous. ECD adds that Theorem 7.4 also implies almost surjectivity on plus rings, independently of [KL15, 3.6.9(c)].
hypotheses: S must be semiperfectoid. BS22 asserts "S is a semiperfectoid ring" without proof. The required input is BMS1 Lemma 3.20, read by the reviewer: if a complete Tate ring R is perfectoid in Fontaine's sense, then every ring of integral elements R^+ is an integral perfectoid ring. Sch12 perfectoid K-algebras are perfectoid in Fontaine's sense (remark after 3.20). S is then a quotient of R^+ and derived p-complete. The proof of 3.20 imports BMS1 Lemmas 3.9-3.10 and [45, Lemma 5.5], none read.

Passing between S_perfd (integral, p-complete) and R' (Tate) needs the ϖ-adic and p-adic topologies on R^+ to agree. This holds when p is a unit of R, since p is then a pseudo-uniformizer; ϖ^p | p alone does not give it. In characteristic p, derived p-completeness is automatic and the ϖ-adic completion of Remark 7.5 must be used. The source does not discuss either case.

ECD's printed remark reads 'S^+ → R^+ is almost surjective'; the mathematically meaningful direction is R^+ → S^+ (almost surjectivity of the plus ring map), as in [KL15, 3.6.9(c)]; recorded as a probable misprint.
proofSteps: Form S = (R^+/(I ∩ R^+))^∧_ϖ; by Theorem 7.4, S → S_perfd is surjective, so R^+ → S_perfd is surjective and R → R' = S_perfd[1/ϖ] is surjective.

Universal property: a continuous map R → T to a perfectoid Tate ring vanishing on I sends R^+ into T° and vanishes on I ∩ R^+, hence induces S → T°. T° is an integral perfectoid ring by BMS1 Lemma 3.20, so this gives S_perfd → T° and then R' → T, which is unique because R → R' is surjective. The integrality and continuity inputs are packet-authored; the source says only "any map from R to a perfectoid ring that vanishes on I factors uniquely over R'".

The vanishing locus of I is therefore Spa(R', R'^+) with R'^+ the minimal open integrally closed subring containing the image of R^+; this is strongly Zariski closed by definition, giving ECD Theorem 5.8 via Definition 5.7.
acceptance: For X = Spa(K⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩, K°⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩) and I = (T): S = (K°⟨T^{1/p^∞}⟩/(T))^∧ and, by the principal case of Theorem 7.4 (T has compatible roots), S_perfd = K°, so R' = K. The Zariski closed subset is the origin Spa(K, K°), and the kernel of R → R' is the closed ideal generated by all T^{1/p^n}, not (T).

Diagonals (for affinoid X = Spa(R, R^+), Y = Spa(S, S^+)): Δ_f is strongly Zariski closed because S ⊗̂_R S → S is surjective, so Δ_f is an immersion (ECD Proposition 5.9). This uses only the definitions, not Theorem 5.8.
